ety.text: From Middle English ruyne, ruine, from Old French ruine, from Latin ruīna (“overthrow, ruin”), from ruō (“to fall down, tumble, sink in ruin, rush”).

senses.d: The remains of a destroyed or dilapidated construction, such as a house or castle.
ex: The labour of a day will not build up a virtuous habit on the ruins of an old and vicious character.
Dr. Manuel: No one is saved. The age of humanity is ended. Soon, only ruin and corpses will remain.

senses.d: The state of being a ruin, destroyed or decayed.
ex: The monastery has fallen into ruin.

senses.d: Something that leads to serious trouble or destruction.
ex: Gambling has been the ruin of many.
The errors of young men are the ruin of business.
His ruin startled th’ other steeds.

senses.d: A change that destroys or defeats something; destruction; overthrow.
ex: the ruin of a ship or an army
the ruin of a constitution or a government

senses.d: To cause the fiscal ruin of; to bankrupt or drive out of business.
ex: With all these purchases, you surely mean to ruin us!

senses.d: To destroy or render something no longer usable or operable.
ex: He ruined his new white slacks by accidentally spilling oil on them.

senses.d: To destroy (e.g. a city) so as to leave ruins.
ex: By the fireside there are old men seated, / Seeing ruined cities in the ashes.

senses.d: To upset or overturn the plans or progress of, or to have a disastrous effect on something.
ex: My car breaking down just as I was on the road ruined my vacation.

senses.d: To make something less enjoyable or likeable.
ex: I used to love that song, but being assaulted when that song was playing ruined the song for me.

senses.d: To make (someone) have a ruined orgasm.
To reveal the ending of (a story); to spoil.
To fall into a state of decay.
ex: Though he his house of polisht marble build, / Yet shall it ruine like the Moth's fraile cell

senses.d: To seduce or debauch, and thus harm the social standing of.
ex: The young libertine was notorious for ruining local girls.
